episodes.description:

We discuss:
1. Why model development is not just engineering, but also like Snape’s potions class
2. Google’s full-stack frontier AI strategy
3. What PMs do inside a frontier AI lab
4. Tulsee’s 60-20-20 framework for balancing what works now and what’s almost working
5. How to write your first eval
6. The rising value of great PMs

episodes.title: How a 19-year-old intern built the growth engine behind this $2B AI company | Hector Serrano
episodes.description:
Hector Serrano runs one of the most innovative and successful paid growth programs in Silicon Valley. As Head of Content at Wispr Flow, a leading AI voice-to-text tool, he built a roster of 50 creators who drive 500 to 600 paid user-generated content (UGC) ads every month. The creators are paid a cut of ad spend, and the best of them earn over $13,000 a month. It’s a playbook the best DTC brands have used for years, now adapted for SaaS. Hector joined Wispr Flow at 19, before the product had PMF, and over the past year, Wispr Flow has grown revenue 30x and raised at a $2 billion valuation.
We discuss:
1. Why paid UGC is one of the biggest untapped growth levers right now
2. The step-by-step playbook for building a successful paid-UGC program
3. Why the best marketers are “allergic to AI”
4. What makes a great modern marketing hire
5. Why YouTube is the most underrated growth lever in SaaS

赫克托·塞拉诺 (Hector Serrano) 运营着硅谷最具创新性和最成功的付费成长计划之一。作为领先的 AI 语音转文本工具 Wispr Flow 的内容主管，他建立了一个由 50 名创作者组成的名单，每月推出 500 至 600 个付费用户生成内容 (UGC) 广告。创作者会从广告支出中获得一定比例的报酬，其中最好的人每月收入超过 13,000 美元。这是最好的 DTC 品牌多年来使用的剧本，现在适用于 SaaS。 Hector 于 19 岁时加入 Wispr Flow，当时该产品还没有 PMF，在过去的一年里，Wispr Flow 的收入增长了 30 倍，估值达到 20 亿美元。
我们讨论：
1. 为什么付费 UGC 是目前尚未开发的最大增长杠杆之一
2. 构建成功的付费 UGC 项目的分步指南
3. 为什么最好的营销人员“对人工智能过敏”
4. 是什么造就了优秀的现代营销人员
5. 为什么 YouTube 是 SaaS 领域最被低估的增长杠杆

episodes.title: An 86-minute guide to finding PMF | Rob Snyder (Author, The Power of Pull)
episodes.description:
Rob Snyder is the author of The Power of Pull and writes the newsletter The Physics of Startups. He has advised more than 50 startups on growing from zero to $1 million in ARR, drawing on his own experience as a founder who spent two years pushing a product the market didn’t want before accidentally stumbling onto what actually works. In this episode, we walk step by step through his framework for finding product-market fit, from coming up with an idea to closing your first handful of deals.
We discuss:
1. The PULL framework: Project, Unavoidable, List of options, Limitations
2. Where the best startup ideas come from
3. Tactics for cold outreach and running your first sales call
4. Why Rob advises against design partners
5. Goblin mode: what to do when nothing is working
6. How to apply the PULL framework inside larger companies
episodes.descriptionCN:
罗布·斯奈德 (Rob Snyder) 是《拉力的力量》一书的作者，也是时事通讯《初创公司的物理学》的作者。他利用自己作为创始人的经验，为 50 多家初创公司提供了从零到 100 万美元的 ARR 增长建议，他花了两年时间推出市场不想要的产品，然后意外地发现了真正有效的产品。在本集中，我们将逐步介绍他寻找产品与市场契合度的框架，从提出想法到完成第一笔交易。
我们讨论：
1. PULL 框架：项目、不可避免的问题、选项列表、限制
2. 最好的创业创意来自哪里
3. 冷外展和第一次销售拜访的策略
4. 为什么 Rob 不建议设计合作伙伴
5.妖精模式：什么都不起作用时该怎么办
6. 如何在大公司内部应用PULL框架

episodes.title: Inside the black box of AI: How AI models actually think | Emmanuel Ameisen (Anthropic)
episodes.description:
Emmanuel Ameisen is an interpretability researcher at Anthropic, where he looks inside LLMs like Claude to understand how they think. Before joining Anthropic, he spent years in applied ML at Stripe and Insight, and is the author of Building Machine Learning Powered Applications. His research has produced some of the most striking findings in the field: that models form general representations of concepts, plan many tokens ahead without stating those plans explicitly, and may exhibit something structurally similar to the distinction between conscious and unconscious processing in humans.
We discuss:
1. Why the “next-token predictor” framing undersells how models actually plan and think
2. Why anthropomorphizing AI can actually be the right approach
3. Why models are “grown,” not built
4. What the “J space” reveals about model self-awareness
5. The smooth scaling curve behind what look like sudden capability jumps
6. How interpretability connects to AI alignment and safety
episodes.descriptionCN:
Emmanuel Ameisen 是 Anthropic 的可解释性研究员，他深入研究像 Claude 这样的法学硕士，以了解他们的想法。在加入 Anthropic 之前，他在 Stripe 和 Insight 从事应用机器学习工作多年，并且是《构建机器学习驱动的应用程序》一书的作者。他的研究产生了该领域一些最引人注目的发现：模型形成概念的一般表示，提前计划许多标记而无需明确说明这些计划，并且可能在结构上表现出类似于人类有意识和无意识处理之间的区别的东西。
我们讨论：
1. 为什么“下一个令牌预测器”框架低估了模型实际计划和思考的方式
2. 为什么人工智能拟人化实际上是正确的方法
3. 为什么模型是“成长”的，而不是构建的
4.“J空间”揭示了模特的自我意识
5.看似突然的能力跳跃背后的平滑缩放曲线
6. 可解释性如何与人工智能一致性和安全性联系起来

episodes.title: Why every company now needs to think and operate like a lab team | Josh Woodward (Google Labs, Gemini, AI Studio)
episodes.description:
Josh Woodward is the head of Google Labs, the Gemini app, and AI Studio. He has spent over 17 years at Google and oversees its longest-running and largest labs team, whose products include NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook), Project Genie, and Flow. His job is to find, experiment with, and scale new AI products, and he has built one of the most distinctive product cultures in the industry for generating ideas, running experiments, and, even more importantly, knowing when to quit.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why every company now needs to think and operate like a labs team
2. Where the best ideas really come from
3. The “almost possible” framework
4. How to recognize genuine product-market fit early
5. When to kill an idea
6. What skills are rising in value in the AI era
7. Why roles are not actually blurring into one universal builder role
8. How to set up your internal labs team
episodes.descriptionCN:
乔什·伍德沃德 (Josh Woodward) 是 Google 实验室、Gemini 应用程序和 AI Studio 的负责人。他在 Google 工作了 17 年多，负责管理其运行时间最长、规模最大的实验室团队，其产品包括 NotebookLM（现为 Gemini Notebook）、Project Genie 和 Flow。他的工作是发现、试验和扩展新的人工智能产品，他建立了业内最独特的产品文化之一，用于产生想法、进行实验，更重要的是，知道何时退出。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 为什么现在每家公司都需要像实验室团队一样思考和运作
2. 最好的想法真正来自哪里
3.“几乎可能”的框架
4. 如何及早识别真正的产品与市场契合度

episodes.title: Designing for Agents — Zeno Rocha, Resend
episodes.description:
A coding agent opens a pull request and picks an email provider for you. How did it choose? Resend co-founder and CEO Zeno Rocha explores answer engine optimization (AEO) through a concrete example: which email provider does Claude Code recommend, and how does that change across model versions? Then comes the agent experience itself. Once the agent picks Resend, can it find the price, set up the account and send its first email?
We also follow an email after the API call succeeds. Zeno explains what happens when Gmail throttles a burst, why a tracking pixel can give you the wrong idea about who opened a message, and how one abusive sender can put other customers’ mail at risk. Then we get into the product decisions: giving an agent 80+ named MCP tools, letting it read pricing in Markdown, and letting it register for a service on its own.

episodes.title: What Frontier Labs Buy: A Data Deep Dive with Handshake AI — Garrett Lord & Team
episodes.description:
Our first deep dive with an AI data company. Handshake AI went from launch to roughly $1 billion in annualized gross revenue in about a year. What are frontier labs actually buying? Garrett Lord and the team open up the reinforcement learning environments behind their expert training data, from biology and investment banking to alignment.
An AI agent found a way to earn credit for net income: open a new Excel tab and fill it with every number from one to a million. The grader found the number it wanted. A banker would have looked for it in the right row, for the right year.
Garrett Lord and the Handshake AI team take Latent Space inside the work of building evaluations for frontier labs. A scientist walks us through a gel and nine brain-tissue slides. A banker follows an agent through its inbox, Python code, and financial model to find the assumption that broke the deal. The safety team shows how to read an agent’s actions when its final answer sounds fine.

The Home Depot's founding story is like an Avengers movie… if the Avengers got fired, went broke, and stacked empty paint cans ten feet high to look legitimate. After being unceremoniously fired from their previous hardware chain at ages 48 and 35, Bernie Marcus and Arthur Blank took the words of their New York banker Ken Langone (who had also just accidentally caused their firings) to heart: they'd just been "kicked in the ass with a golden horseshoe.” They proceeded to author the greatest compounding story in American retail history, helped by some legendary cameos along the way from Sol Price, Jamie Dimon, and Ross Perot (to name a few). episodes.title: Disney: The Renaissance and the Empire (Audio)
episodes.description:
In 1984, the Walt Disney Company was worth more dead than alive. Disney Animation — the heart of Walt's famous flywheel — had stagnated for years, bleeding away talent while corporate raiders circled, salivating over offers to sell off the film library to MGM and offload the parks to hotel operators. But what followed instead was the greatest turnaround in media history under Michael Eisner and Frank Wells. Beauty and the Beast. The Lion King. Broadway. Bringing the Disney Vault home on VHS and DVD. And the greatest media acquisition of all time — ESPN.
And then... it all almost fell apart. Again. Euro Disney turned into a money pit. Boardroom and executive infighting ran rampant. Animation descended into a dumpster fire. (Remember Chicken Little? Us neither.) Comcast — Comcast!! — tried to steal the company via a hostile takeover. Out of the chaos, a new generation of Disney management emerged under Bob Iger to stage yet another epic comeback with Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm, creating the defining media empire of the 21st century…until the tech companies came along. Tune in for the ultimate Acquired thrill ride: Disney, Part II.

episodes.title: AI Software Factories
episodes.description:
“Clearly there are 100x or 1,000x engineers now. The world hasn’t adjusted.”
— Guillermo Rauch (Vercel)
Guillermo: I’ve been really pilled with this idea of software factories. You used to ship the output directly, and everything inside the company was how good is person A at shipping output B? And now what’s happening is the way that I’m judging you as an engineer is, are you producing the factory that will produce multiplicative outputs B through Z, right?
We used to believe, and it used to be somewhat controversial, that there’s 10X engineers. Now clearly there’s 100X or 1,000X engineers. And the world hasn’t fully adjusted to this.
@naval: I used to get flamed on Twitter for saying there are 10X engineers, because it flies in the face of so much equality philosophy that everyone’s equal. But the reality is, when you’re operating in idea domains—when you’re operating in intellectual domains and virtual digital domains—it’s not even 10X. It’s 100X or 1,000X, and it always has been.
Satoshi, Notch, the guy who invented JavaScript, the Brendan Eichs of the world. John Carmack. These are 1,000X programmers.
Not to even mention if you choose the right thing to work on versus the wrong thing to work on, that’s an infinity difference. And it could just be not necessarily even a better programmer, just one who had a better judgment of what to work on in the first place.
And now obviously it’s less controversial, because of AI leverage.
episodes.descriptionCN:
“显然现在有 100 倍或 1,000 倍的工程师。世界还没有调整。”
— 吉列尔莫·劳赫 (Vercel)
Guillermo：我对软件工厂的想法非常着迷。你以前直接运送输出，公司内部的一切都是A在运送输出B时有多好？现在发生的事情是我对你作为一名工程师的评价，你是否正在生产将产生乘法输出 B 到 Z 的工厂，对吗？
我们曾经相信，有 10X 工程师的存在，但也曾经存在一些争议。现在显然有 100 倍或 1,000 倍的工程师。世界还没有完全适应这一点。
@naval：我曾经因为说有 10X 工程师而在 Twitter 上受到攻击，因为它违背了人人平等的平等理念。但现实是，当你在创意领域运作时——当你在知识领域和虚拟数字领域运作时——它甚至不是 10 倍。它是 100 倍或 1,000 倍，而且一直都是。
Satoshi，Notch，JavaScript 的发明者，世界上的 Brendan Eichs。约翰·卡马克.这些是 1000 倍的程序员。
更不用说你选择正确的工作还是错误的工作，这是一个无穷大的差异。而且不一定是更好的程序员，只是一个对首先要做什么有更好判断的人。
现在，由于人工智能的影响力，它的争议显然减少了。

I sit down with Nick, co-founder of Orgo, to break down how to build a custom Grok Bot for a business and sell it for $25,000 up front with a $3,000-a-month retainer. Nick demos Bops, the agent platform he built in a 36-hour weekend, where each bot has its own phone number, email, and computer with four screens. He walks me through his research, design, and build process, the stack behind each bot, and the offer he takes to business owners. We also cover how to pick a niche by calling 50 people you know and how to turn one free case study into warm referrals. If you want to sell AI employees to businesses, this episode gives you the stack, the offer, and an open source repo you can fork today.

• Busy owners want their problems solved, so a GrokBot built for their industry wins over a platform they have to set up.
• Nick builds in three steps: research the category, design in Paper, then pick a stack and read the docs.
• Each bot gets its own email, phone number, computer, and connectors through Agent Mail, Agent Phone, Orgo, and Composio.
• The SMB offer is $25,000 up front for a system the owner keeps, plus an optional $3,000-a-month retainer.
• A free website redesign, a money-back guarantee, and free lead magnets make the offer easy to accept.
• Call 50 people you know, do the first build free, and trade the case study for warm intros.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. Why Businesses Want a Custom GrokBot
Nick built Bops, short for business ops, as a GrokBot clone in a weekend, and his demo video got 75K views on Twitter. I see the price of software trending toward zero, with the money in upselling agents and human intelligence, and Nick sees purpose-built apps for one business taking off. Owners are too busy to set up GrokBot or Dots themselves, so Nick ships agents pre-built for an industry like insurance or dental clinics, each with its own phone number, email, and Slack connector.
2. Research, Design, Build
Nick built Bops in one long-running T3 Code thread with Opus 5.5 over 36 hours, with loops running overnight. He starts by having the model research GrokBot, Meta's Muse, and OpenAI's Dots, then designs in Paper through the Paper MCP, asking for three or four variations and combining the best parts, a process he calls diverge and then converge. He tried T3 Code after seeing Theo's content on Twitter and likes that it is simple, free, and works with a Claude subscription.
3. The Stack Behind Each Bot
Orgo provides each bot's computer, Agent Mail its email, Agent Phone its phone number, and Composio its connectors through one API connection. For every feature, Nick tells his agent to read the docs and the API references, then sends CleanShot screenshots of bugs or of GrokBot UI elements he likes, and I keep a swipe file of references for the same job. Bops gives each bot a full computer for privacy and multitasking, where GrokBot gives each bot a screen, and Nick hosts on Orgo, Fly, or Vercel and ships fast.
4. The $25,000 Offer
For SMBs, Nick sells the system for $25,000 up front, maybe collected in two halves, then offers an optional $3,000-a-month retainer after a 30-day implementation. When I play a dental clinic owner and ask about the return, Nick compares one bot to a front desk hire at $50,000 to $70,000 a year, out of 15 bots the owner keeps. Owners like owning the system over feeling held by the neck on a retainer for AI employees.
8. Landing the First Clients
Nick suggests calling 50 people you know who run a business or work high up in one, then doing the first build free for a case study, which is how he found the promotional products industry. Shadow that first client while they share their screen on manual work like invoices, and the right agents become clear. I'd frame the free build as a $50,000-a-year service and ask for intros to three local peers in return

episodes.title: SaaS is dead?
episodes.description:
In this solo episode, I explain why I say SaaS is dead and what I see taking its place. For 15 years, SaaS meant paying engineers to build a tool and charging per seat, and now models like Opus 5.5, GPT-6, and Argon make the tool easy to build. I walk through what I call smart SaaS: give the tool away for free, collect data and network effects, and make money by upselling AI agents and human services. I share a calorie tracking example, three ways to charge, and why enterprises still pay per seat. If you build software, this episode gives you a map for building something people want in a market where the tool is free.
Timestamps
00:00 – Intro
00:47 – SaaS 1.0
02:56 – SaaS 2.0: The New Business Model
05:12 – How to monetize SaaS 2.0
06:18 – Service is the new Software
07:22 – SaaS Is Dead, Long Live SaaS
08:58 – SMB vs Enterprise
10:31 – Closing Thoughts
Key Points
• AI makes the tool easy to build, so the per-seat model of the last 15 years has run its course.
• Smart SaaS gives the tool away and collects data and network effects as payment.
• The money comes from upselling intelligence from AI agents and services from humans.
• Agents can charge by token or by outcome, and human services by the week or month.
• SaaS for SMBs, prosumers, and individuals trends toward free, while enterprises still pay something per seat.
• The market for getting things done is bigger than the market for tools, so the total market for SaaS grows.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. How SaaS Worked
For the last 15 years, the hard part of SaaS was getting enough smart engineers in a room to code a high-quality tool for a human to use. Customers paid per seat, at prices like $9.99 or $29.99, to use that tool in the cloud. The model made people billions of dollars, and Slack, which I believe sold for $29 billion, shows how well it worked.
2. AI Makes the Tool Easy
Models at the level of Opus 5.5, GPT-6, Astra, Argon, and Carbon make building the software easy. One or two people with AI can now build what used to take a team of 20, so charging per seat for a tool stops working.
3. Give the Tool Away
In smart SaaS, I still build a tool, and I give it away for free: the CRM, the dashboard, the app. I look for niches where people pay for a tool in the old model and hand them that tool at zero cost. Users pay with data, which I can sell or use to make the tool better, and with network effects that build a moat.
4. Upselling Intelligence
I call the old model dumb SaaS because it is only a tool, and the new model smart SaaS because it is intelligent. With a free CRM, I charge when the customer wants AI agents to do work in it, or I upsell a service delivered by humans, which lines up with Sequoia's view of trillion-dollar services as the new software. A calorie tracking app can give away the tracker, charge for agents that build personalized meal plans or track calories more precisely, and sell a weekly weight coach.
5. A Product Studio of Free Tools
Per-seat pricing limited the market, since only some people want to pay for tools. I see a product studio built around free tools, with upsells to agents or humans, as a way into the many niches that are wide open right now. That is why I say SaaS is dead, long live SaaS.
6. Pricing Agents and Services
Agents can charge by token or by outcome, so the customer pays when the agents complete the work. Human services can charge a weekly or monthly fee. The market for people accomplishing things is bigger than the market for people using a tool, so I see the total market for SaaS growing.
7. Where Enterprises Fit
SaaS for SMBs, prosumers, and individuals trends toward free. Fortune 500 and Fortune 2000 companies may still pay something per seat, a number I expect to drop over time, plus upsells to humans and superintelligence. Some enterprises want to pay for the security and for the feeling of being taken care of.

• Strong harness ideas sit in subjective work, where people care about the output and want a human in the loop.
• Your edge comes from a distinct vision, proprietary data, or a business that mixes AI with the physical world.
• Gamma gets 98% of its value from prompts and treats fine-tuning as a cost and quality optimization.
• Experiments reward volume, and Gamma's fast mode test showed that good friction raised paid conversion.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. What is an Agent Harness
Gamma started in 2020, took off in 2023, and spent this year rebuilding its product from preset LLM workflows into an agent. Jon defines the harness as the tools an agent uses to act in its environment, inspect its own work, and ask the user for preferences, with Claude Code as the best-known example for programming. I call harnesses the new wrappers, and Jon agrees, since the wrapping is most of the work and even OpenAI and Anthropic put heavy effort into harness development.
2. Inside One Gamma Prompt
When someone pastes messy notes and asks for 20 slides, Gamma spins up a cloud sandbox, asks a few questions through a form, and pulls context from Notion, Slack, or Linear. It writes an outline, picks a template with vision models and embedding search, then generates text, layouts, images, and charts in parallel in about a minute. A vision model checks every slide for misaligned text, cropped heads, and weak contrast, and after rounds of fixes the deck has used about 20 models and 200 calls.
3. Where Vertical Harnesses Fit
Jon looks for problems that differ from coding: subjective work where people disagree on what good looks like and care about the specifics of the output. He likes personal video games for non-technical players and sees physical services, legal tech, and medical tech as active areas, though I'd pass on legal tech today because it feels crowded. Jon names three kinds of edge: a distinct vision you move toward faster, proprietary data, and businesses that mix AI with hardware or real-life services.
4. Image Models, Niches, and Loving the Work
Jon calls AI image models underhyped, since most people use them for menus and logos while Gamma uses about 10 image models for diagrams, textures, and icons. A couch shopping harness could render a couch in your room, measure it in pixels to tell a 58-inch from a 68-inch fit, and suggest a better option, with interior designers and pros at companies like Restoration Hardware as durable buyers. Jon closes with advice to pick work you could dogfood eight hours a day, and I add my rule to marry the niche and date the product.

In this solo episode, I break down the war on AI agents, from Amazon blocking Meta's Muse to Delta treating outside booking agents as unauthorized automated activity to Yelp charging agents for access. I share how I think about an agent, as a customer with a credit card who reads your site instead of looking at it, and the ladder of trust that runs from research to prepare to pay. Then I walk through each big player's bet, my nine stages for how this war plays out, five moves any business can make this week, and the startup ideas I see between agents and the businesses they buy from. If you run a store or build products, this episode gives you a map for selling to customers who send an agent to shop for them.

Key Points
• Agents read product details, prices, shipping, and return policies, so plain-text facts on the page decide whether they pick you.
• Agents climb a ladder of trust from research to prepare to pay, and the whole fight happens on the pay rung.
• Many blocks protect the ad and upsell revenue that agents skip on the way to the sale.
• The biggest stores block, the biggest audiences open the door, and payment and security companies want the toll booth.
• I expect a Plaid moment for agent identity and payments, followed later by ads that buy an agent's first recommendation.
• Vertical Plaids, agent insurance, and agent analytics are open lanes for startups right now.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. Who Blocks and Who Welcomes
Amazon started blocking Meta's Muse agent around September, Delta treats outside booking agents as unauthorized automated activity, and Yelp lets agents in only through its paid data licensing program. In the middle, Zillow welcomes agents acting for real customers while its anti-scraping tools sometimes stop them, and Walmart, a Muse partner, called its Muse failures an accident. On the welcoming side, Meta works with Walmart and Stripe on an open standard, Shopify lets merchants sell through AI channels, and Visa and Mastercard build ways to recognize trusted agents.
2. A Customer Who Reads Instead of Looks
I think of an agent as a customer with a credit card who reads instead of looks. It skips your $100,000 homepage video, banners, and countdown pop-ups, and it reads your product details, prices, shipping costs, and return policy. When I ask my agent to find a replacement air purifier filter, compare delivered prices, and check with me before buying anything over $50, I give it a goal, rules, and a limit.
3. The Ladder of Trust
Agents climb three rungs: research, prepare, and pay. Most companies accept the first rung because it works like search, and the whole war happens on the third, so I see businesses making a mistake when they block all three. An agent compares five suppliers in the time it takes me to open one tab and stays loyal to whatever worked last time, so a stuck checkout quietly sends it to a competitor.
4. Why Companies Block
Some reasons to block hold up, since an agent might place 50 orders instead of five, the customer calls the store about it, and an airline has to prove you authorized a booking. Money drives a lot of it, because Amazon earns tens of billions a year from ads and airlines profit from seat upgrades, bags, and credit card offers that agents skip. Amazon and Delta also build their own agents
5. The 9 Stages
Banks fought Mint.com until Plaid built a proper connection between apps and banks, and the banks moved from blocking to signing deals to charging for access. I see agents on that same path, from blocking today to an arms race to a split where sales businesses let agents in, data businesses charge, and giants build their own, then a Plaid moment for agent identity and payments. After that, welcoming companies win customers, everyone competes for agents with faster checkouts and pages written for agents, ads come back to buy an agent's first recommendation

在这一集中，我详细分析了针对人工智能代理的战争，从亚马逊封锁 Meta 的 Muse，到达美航空将外部预订代理视为未经授权的自动化活动，再到 Yelp 向代理收取访问费用。我分享了我对代理商的看法，即作为持有信用卡的客户，他们会阅读您的网站而不是查看网站，以及从研究到准备付款的信任阶梯。然后我会详细介绍每个大玩家的赌注、我对这场战争如何展开的九个阶段、任何企业本周可以采取的五项举措，以及我在代理商和他们购买的企业之间看到的创业想法。如果您经营一家商店或生产产品，本集将为您提供一张向客户销售的地图，这些客户派出代理商为他们购物。

要点
• 代理商会阅读产品详细信息、价格、运输和退货政策，因此页面上的纯文本事实决定他们是否会选择您。
• 代理商从研究到准备付款，沿着信任的阶梯向上爬，整个斗争都发生在薪酬梯级上。
• 许多块可以保护代理商在销售过程中跳过的广告和追加销售收入。
• 最大的商店街区、最多的观众开门、支付和安全公司想要收费站。
• 我预计代理身份和付款会出现格子图案，随后会出现购买代理第一个推荐的广告。
• 垂直格子、代理保险和代理分析现在为初创公司敞开了大门。
编号部分摘要
1. 谁阻挡谁欢迎
亚马逊在 9 月份左右开始屏蔽 Meta 的 Muse 代理，达美航空将外部预订代理视为未经授权的自动化活动，而 Yelp 仅通过其付费数据许可计划允许代理进入。中间，Zillow 欢迎代表真实客户的代理，而其反抓取工具有时会阻止他们，Muse 合作伙伴沃尔玛称其 Muse 失败是一次意外。在受欢迎的方面，Meta 与沃尔玛和 Stripe 合作采用开放标准，Shopify 允许商家通过人工智能渠道进行销售，Visa 和 Mastercard 建立了识别可信代理商的方法。
2. 阅读而不是观看的顾客
我认为代理就像是持有信用卡的顾客，他们会阅读而不是看。它会跳过您价值 100,000 美元的主页视频、横幅和倒计时弹出窗口，并读取您的产品详细信息、价格、运费和退货政策。当我要求我的代理商寻找替换的空气净化器过滤器，比较交付的价格，并在购买超过 50 美元的东西之前与我核实时，我给了它一个目标、规则和限制。
3. 信任的阶梯
特工要攀登三级：研究、准备和支付。大多数公司接受第一级，因为它的工作原理类似于搜索，而整个战争发生在第三级，所以我认为企业在阻止所有三级时会犯错误。一名代理商在我打开一个选项卡的时间内就比较了五个供应商，并忠于上次有效的产品，因此结帐停滞会悄悄地将其发送给竞争对手。
4. 为什么公司会封锁
阻止等待的一些原因，因为代理可能会下 50 个订单而不是 5 个，客户会致电商店询问此事，航空公司必须证明您授权了预订。金钱是其中的重要推动力，因为亚马逊每年从广告中赚取数百亿美元，而航空公司则从代理商跳过的座位升级、行李和信用卡优惠中获利。亚马逊和达美也建立了自己的代理
5. 9个阶段
银行与 Mint.com 展开斗争，直到 Plaid 在应用程序和银行之间建立了适���的连接，银行从封锁转向签署协议，再到对访问收费。我看到代理商也走上了同样的道路，从今天的封锁到军备竞赛，再到销售企业让代理商进入、数据业务收费、巨头们建立自己的分裂，然后是代理商身份和支付的格子时刻。之后，欢迎公司赢得客户，每个人都以更快的结账速度和为代理商编写的页面来争夺代理商，广告回来购买代理商的第一个推荐
